items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The habitual and controlled use of fire among Neanderthal groups, together with the residential use of caves and rock shelters, represents a major turning point in the emergence of Paleolithic camp bases. In Middle Paleolithic sites, the interrelation between shelter geomorphology, fire-use locations and activity areas has been interpreted as evidence of spatial organization. Hearths are, therefore, valuable for investigating site structure. The Abric Romaní offers an exceptional case study due to the preservation and extensive excavation strategy of numerous combustion structures across several archaeological units. This study analyses fire-use spatial organization in units Nb, Oa, Ob, P, Qa and R (ca. 60–54 ka) to explore how Neanderthals structured their living spaces. Using spatial statistical methods (i.e., covariate analysis, spatial modelling, and mark analysis), we evaluate the influence of distance from the back wall on fire-use location and distribution. We then isolate this effect to examine micro-scale patterns and compare the morphological and functional characteristics of combustion structures between wall-adjacent and wall-distanced sectors and across the archaeological sequence. Our findings show a relationship between fire-use locations and the back wall, defining preferential zones for fire placement. Fire use reflects a structured spatial zoning, separating combustion structures in sleeping and resting areas from those in communal activity areas. The morphology of combustion structures remained stable across units, while fire use varied flexibly within a stable spatial framework. Overall, these findings suggest that late Neanderthal occupations at Abric Romaní exhibited structured spatial cultural patterns comparable to those documented in modern hunter-gatherer campsites.</jats:p>
items.summary: 《通过燃烧结构空间组织识别中旧石器时代居住单元》：该研究以西班牙巴塞罗那阿布里克罗曼尼遗址约6万至5.4万年前的多个考古单元为对象，运用空间统计方法分析火塘位置与后壁距离的关系，发现火的使用呈现有结构的空间分区，睡眠休息区与公共活动区的燃烧结构相分离，为理解尼安德特人居住空间组织提供了新证据。
items.title: Identifying Middle Paleolithic Residential Units Through the Spatial Organization of Combustion Structures at Abric Romaní (Barcelona, Spain)

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    This study investigates the ecology of the extinct European
                    <jats:italic>Hippopotamus</jats:italic>
                    from the late Early–Middle Pleistocene (
                    <jats:italic>c</jats:italic>
                    . 900–400 ka) sequence of the Megalopolis Basin, a glacial microrefugium for temperate taxa in southern Greece. Using stable carbon (δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C) and oxygen (δ
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                    O) isotope analyses and microwear analyses of
                    <jats:italic>Hippopotamus</jats:italic>
                    dental elements, we reconstruct dietary variability, past habitat conditions and hydrological or climatic changes at intra‐annual, multi‐annual and millennial scales. The results indicate the dominance of C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    woodland/mesic grassland environments throughout the examined period and jointly suggest a broader aridification trend from MIS 16 to MIS 12. The studied individuals followed a browsing to mixed‐feeding diet and exhibited seasonally variable dietary habits. They also record potential short‐term climatic or hydrological shifts, which likely further impacted habitat or resource availability in the area. The incidence of enamel hypoplasia in early Middle Pleistocene specimens, which is tentatively correlated to cooler conditions, shows that the taxon survived in the region even during stressful, less optimal periods. These findings provide a crucial framework to better understand the ecological niche of the species, as well as the impact of dynamic ecosystems on adaptations of large mammals, including hominins, in the European Middle Pleistocene.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Effrosyni Roditi, Gabriele Russo, Hervé Bocherens, George E. Konidaris, Athanassios Athanassiou, Florent Rivals, Vangelis Tourloukis, Eleni Panagopoulou, Panagiotis Karkanas, Katerina Harvati

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Benthic suspension feeders have long been thought to depend solely on particulate organic matter (POM) for their nutritional needs. Our research, conducted in the Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea), shows that the available concentration of planktonic carbon in the reef water is too low to meet the metabolic demands (measured through in situ oxygen uptake) of common bivalves (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Spondylus</jats:italic>
                    sp. and
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Chama pacifica</jats:italic>
                    ) and ascidians (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Polycarpa mytiligera</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Halocynthia spinosa</jats:italic>
                    ). In situ measurements confirmed a concentration-dependent uptake of bulk dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and protein-like dissolved organic compounds (fDOM, analyzed via spectrofluorometry) by
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Spondylus</jats:italic>
                    sp. and
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">P. mytiligera</jats:italic>
                    , suggesting that DOC uptake may balance their carbon budgets. Stable isotope (δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C) mixing models indicate that reef-derived DOC (mean δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C = −18.4 ± 0.7‰) emerges as the primary carbon source for bivalves (57% of their body composition), far surpassing contributions from particulate sources (26% from POC > 100 µm and 14% from POC < 100 µm). While ascidians still rely primarily on POM (60 to 71%), DOC plays an essential role as a supplementary food source (23 to 29%). These results challenge the prevailing assumption that POM is the exclusive food source for these organisms. Given the widespread presence of bivalves and ascidians in benthic habitats, our findings highlight their ability to bypass the microbial loop and directly utilize dissolved organic compounds, prompting a reevaluation of current benthic carbon budgets.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Understanding how foraging behavior and diet influence individual reproductive success is a key interest in evolutionary ecology. This is particularly true for capital breeding species where the accumulation and storage of energy to support offspring is critical, often following the “bigger‐is‐better” hypothesis. Using data collected from female gray seals (
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:italic>Halichoerus grypus</jats:italic>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    ) at Sable Island, Canada, between 1995 and 2018, we tested the hypothesis that differences in foraging effort and diet prior to the breeding season, estimated through satellite telemetry, stable isotope (SI) signatures, and quantitative fatty acid signature analysis (QFASA), respectively, affect reproductive success. There was no relationship between dominant prey type, the energy density of estimated diets, and maternal postpartum mass (MPPM). Females consuming a diet of lower diversity and with more positive δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C estimates, possibly indicating more benthic foraging, had higher MPPM. MPPM was the best predictor of offspring mass at weaning. However, metrics of maternal foraging effort and diet alone did not influence pup weaning mass when MPPM was included in the model. These results suggest that different foraging strategies and diets can lead to sufficient body energy storage that enables reproductive success in a capital breeder. Considering this colony was increasing rapidly during the study period, the influence of foraging effort and diet might differ in a stable or declining population where intraspecific competition may be more evident.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The mouse (
                    <jats:italic>Mus musculus</jats:italic>
                    ) pelvis features an elongated ilium and triangular pubis and ischium characteristic of a small quadruped, whereas humans possess a short, broad, bowl‐shaped pelvis specialized for bipedal locomotion and childbirth. Mice are widely used to model osteoporosis, hip dysplasia, and other pelvic pathologies, yet
                    <jats:italic>in utero</jats:italic>
                    mouse pelvic development has been incompletely characterized, limiting cross‐species interpretation. Here, we integrate 3D micro‐CT and histology to generate a comprehensive atlas of mouse pelvic development from embryonic days 12.5–18.5 (E12.5–E18.5), focusing on the ilium, hip joint, and sacroiliac joint. We show that E14.5 is a critical stage, when the hip and sacroiliac joints form. We identify a sequential developmental program in mice in which joint cartilage forms first, followed by muscle‐cartilage interaction, and, subsequently, extensive blood vessel growth. In contrast to the transversely oriented, developmentally delayed iliac growth and ossification described in recent studies of the human bipedal pelvis, the mouse ilium follows an earlier, centrally initiated, longitudinal ossification pattern. Overall, our atlas provides an essential quadrupedal reference for interpreting human pelvic development, evolution, and disease models.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Serena C. Fernandopulle, Mark A. Wright, Nina St. Hillaire, Anika Liv Christensen, Stephanie E. Pierce, Gayani Senevirathne, Terence D. Capellini

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lake Woods, Jurrkulu, is northern Australia's largest freshwater lake filled today in strong Indo–Australian summer monsoons (IASM) to maximum depths of ~5 m. On the western margins of the lake, two large arcuate ridges occur 20 to 40 m above the lake floor and inset within these are other mid‐elevation lake deposits, such as depositional ridges, which suggest past filling events much higher than the modern maximum. We have undertaken the analysis of 20 samples for single‐grain optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) from shoreline and lake‐floor deposits and supplemented this chronology with an analysis of the basin hypsometry, basin‐wide erosion rates and rare earth elements to ascertain the dominant source of the large source‐bordering ridges. The outer and inner arcuate ridges represent both aeolian accumulation and inferred lake‐level highstands due to the presence of fine gravel facies and gastropods contained within them. We document two lake highstands at 195 ± 16 ka and at 98 ± 7 ka (20 and 15 m above the lake floor, respectively; the lake floor is 197 m Australian Height Datum, AHD). We also present a third but undated filling event 18.5 m above the lake floor (215.5 m AHD) but that is bracketed by two OSL ages of 91 ± 5 and 52 ± 3 ka, with a Bayesian modelled boundary age for lake filling of 95.9 to 53.8 ka (95% credible interval; C.I.). We find no evidence of the previously reported late Marine Isotope Stage [MIS] 3 highstand deposits and the prevalence of gully‐filled structureless sediments, dated to the mid to late Holocene, many of which contain archaeological artefacts that do not allow for the quantification of any accurate Holocene lake‐filling episodes. The lake floor is characterised by deeply cracking silts and clays, with single‐grain OSL results supporting significant post‐depositional mixing (maximum ages are <143 ka). Denudation rate data from detrital stream sediment samples indicate some of the lowest rates of denudation in northern Australia, of between 2.05 ± 0.51 and 0.83 ± 0.23 m/Myr, with the latter rate stemming from the dominant catchment area in the Barkly Tablelands. Sediment provenance data indicate that the slowly eroding Barkly Tablelands is the dominant source for the clays and silts in the lake basin. Despite being the largest lake in northern Australia, the slow rates of catchment‐wide erosion coupled with the intermittent filling have only produced a discontinuous record of the IASM, but one that shows exceptional episodic filling in MIS 5 to 4.</jats:p>

items.abstract: Résumé La Caune de l’Arago est un site emblématique du Pléistocène moyen en Europe occidentale car il a livré un grand nombre de restes humains associés à une industrie lithique très riche et à un assemblage faunique varié et abondant, unique pour la période comprise entre 560 et 400 ka. Les variations stratigraphiques, granulométriques, minéralogiques, pétrographiques, géochimiques, microstructurales et de susceptibilité magnétique permettent de subdiviser ce puissant remplissage en quatre Complexes stratigraphiques, eux-mêmes subdivisés en Séquences et Ensembles. De nombreuses datations effectuées sur ce remplissage finement stratifié ont contribué à l’établissement d’un cadre chronostratigraphique solide tenant compte des différentes phases d’altération et de la composition des niveaux successifs d’occupation humaine. C’est l’un des seuls sites où les datations peuvent être comparées à une faune très riche permettant de contraindre les âges ou à tout le moins de les assimiler à des périodes froides et sèches ou tempérées et humides.
